newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Tough Hyundai workers are now model employees.
newsitem.headline: Tough Hyundai workers are now model employees.

text.p: It took an amphibious assault by thousands of riot police to dislodge striking Hyundai shipyard hands in 1989, but South Korea's toughest workers have now turned into model employees.
On Wednesday the same workers that once rolled flaming oil barrels at riot police to keep them out of South Korea's biggest shipyard were using bulldozers to fight their way in.
They ran a gauntlet of striking unionists at the gates of the giant facility to keep the dockyard open. Later, they used bulldozers to smash down barricades at the entrance.
Picketers lashed out with fists and sloshed buckets of yellow paint over strike-breakers clad in blue overalls.
But there was no stopping the workers who once had a fearsome reputation as the shock troops of a union army that went to war with South Korea's police battalions in an infamous episode in 1989.
Welders, fitters, engineers and crane operators worked normally on Wednesday.
Eight years ago hard-core unionists occupied the control cabins of towering shipyard cranes.
They rampaged through the dockyard sabotaging expensive equipment and took over administrative offices in a 109-day stoppage, one of the longest in South Korean history.
Union leaders had studied military tactics and surprised police with an armoured assault involving bulldozers, cranes, excavators and giant metal-cutting and sanding machines.
During street clashes, workers set fire to 50-gallon oil drums and rolled them at police ranks. Streets were littered with nuts and bolts used as missiles by strikers.
Police counter-attacked at dawn. Inflatable dinghies with crack riot officers on board skimmed over the waves to dockyard wharves while helicopters overhead directed operations.

"The average age of the workers is now more than 40 and they're less militant," said Jin Il-ju, a union official at Hyundai Heavy Industries, explaining why Hyundai workers ignored Wednesday's national strike call.
"They're also comparatively well paid."
Across South Korea, union officials tell a similar story.

Workers that manned the barricades in the late 1980s in a fight for decent wages and working conditions are enjoying the spoils of victory, and have little appetite for the current battle over a new labour law.

Union officials say management at Hyundai Group, an industrial conglomerate that makes everything from ships to computer chips, has since won over workers by awarding generous pay increases and holiday entitlements.
National pay rises have averaged 15 percent over the past decade.
"Because of past bad experiences, management has adopted many tactics to break the union," said Jin.
Hyundai Heavy employs 27,000 workers, of which 21,000 are union members.
"The perception is spreading among the workers that if they down tools the company will face great difficulties," said Jung Jae-heon, a senior manager.
A guard at the dockyard gates said: "We understand and sympathise with what the strikers are saying and doing, but we have to follow company orders.
